title: How is the area left after cutting a piece written?
description: A piece of width four is cut off a rectangle of height n and width twelve. The area left is found from the width that remains, and again by taking the cut piece from the whole. Keeko's doubt is that twelve n minus four n is eight with no n left.
teaching_notes: One idea: twelve n minus four n is eight n, because the letter-number n stays when like terms are subtracted. Watch for students who subtract the numbers and drop the letter.

source: A rectangle ABCD of height n and width 12 has a piece EBCF o
video_script.why: A learner sees that subtracting like terms keeps the letter-number.
video_script.substitution: the book's rectangle ABCD of height n and width twelve with a piece of width four cut off, checked with n as two
video_script.anchor: the rectangle ABCD of the book with height n, width twelve and the cut piece EBCF of width four
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko subtracts the numbers twelve and four and drops the letter. The letter-number n stays in the answer, so the idea is broken with n as two.
video_script.payoff_line: The area left is eight n, and twelve n minus four n equals eight n

final_answer.spoken: eight n, and twelve n minus four n equals eight n; twelve n and minus four n are like terms

maths_rules: area of a rectangle = width x height
way 1: width left = 12 - 4 = 8, so area = 8 x n = 8n
way 2: area of ABCD is 12n, area of EBCF is 4n, so area left = 12n - 4n
12n and -4n have the same letter-number n, so they are like terms
18c and 11d have different letter-numbers, so they are unlike terms
check with n = 2: 12 x 2 - 4 x 2 = 24 - 8 = 16 and 8 x 2 = 16
Keeko test with n = 2: 8 is not 16
video_script.design: The rectangle with its cut piece stays on the board; the area left is found from the width left and by taking the piece from the whole, and the two results are set equal.

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is the next area question in your book.
<bookmark mark='size'/>A rectangle has height n and width twelve.
<bookmark mark='cut'/>A piece of width four is cut off, and the part AEFD is left.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>The book wants the area of the part that is left, in two ways. What will it be?

beats.on_screen: the rectangle with its cut piece stays on the board
narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: rectangle ABCD with area 12 × n = 12n and the piece EBCF with area 4 × n = 4n

marks.whole: the whole rectangle is lit with area 12n
marks.piece: the cut piece is lit with area 4n
marks.left: the part that is left is lit

narration: <bookmark mark='whole'/>The whole rectangle has width twelve and height n, so its area is twelve n.
<bookmark mark='piece'/>The cut piece has width four, so its area is four n.
<bookmark mark='left'/>The part that is left is the whole with the piece taken away.

beats.on_screen: Given: ABCD has height n and width 12; piece EBCF has width 4
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a rectangle of height n and width twelve, with a piece of width four cut off.

beats.on_screen: To find: the area of AEFD in two ways, and which terms are like terms

marks.find: the words area of AEFD in two ways are written
marks.then: the words which terms are alike are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the area of the part left, in two ways.
<bookmark mark='then'/>Then we see which terms are alike.

beats.on_screen: Step 1, way 1, use the width left: 12 − 4 = 8, so area = 8 × n = 8n

marks.width: the width 12 − 4 = 8 is marked along the bottom

narration: <bookmark mark='width'/>Step one, use the width that is left, which is twelve minus four, or eight.
<bookmark mark='area'/>The area is eight times n, which is eight n.

beats.on_screen: Step 2, way 2, take the piece from the whole: 12n − 4n

marks.take: the area 4n is taken away from 12n

narration: <bookmark mark='take'/>Step two, take the area of the piece from the area of the whole.
<bookmark mark='line'/>The area is twelve n minus four n.

beats.on_screen: Step 3, both ways give one area: 12n − 4n = 8n; 12n and −4n are like terms; 18c and 11d are unlike terms; check n = 2: 24 − 8 = 16 and 8 × 2 = 16

marks.same: the two results are joined by an equals sign
marks.name: 12n and −4n are circled and the words like terms are written; 18c and 11d are marked unlike terms
marks.check: 2 replaces n and both sides show 16

narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>Step three, both ways give the same area, so twelve n minus four n is eight n.
<bookmark mark='name'/>Twelve n and minus four n have the same letter-number n. We call such terms like terms. Eighteen c and eleven d are called unlike terms.
<bookmark mark='check'/>Check with n as two. Twenty four minus eight is sixteen, and eight times two is sixteen.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 8n, and 12n − 4n = 8n; 12n and −4n are like terms
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The area left is eight n, and twelve n minus four n equals eight n.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the rectangle
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 12n − 4n = 8, struck out; the test n = 2 gives 16 and 8

marks.gap: 16 and 8 appear side by side and do not match
marks.fix: the bubble is struck out and 8n stays

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks twelve n minus four n is eight with no n left. Twelve minus four is eight.
<bookmark mark='test'/>Try n as two.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>Twenty four minus eight is sixteen, but that idea gives only eight.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The letter-number n is still there, so the answer is eight n.
